content: Neonatal sepsis is a significant contributor to both illness and death in newborns, ranking as the third leading cause of neonatal mortality worldwide and accounting for 13% of all neonatal deaths. Despite its substantial impact, there is a notable lack of high-quality evidence regarding its diagnosis and treatment. This scarcity may be attributed to the diagnostic complexities of sepsis and the relative immunosuppression observed in neonates. Consequently, many newborns are administered antibiotics based on suspicion of sepsis. Antibiotics are now the most frequently used medications in neonatal intensive care units. The last Cochrane Review on this topic was updated in 2004, underscoring the need for a more current systematic review to evaluate the effects of various antibiotic regimens for early-onset neonatal sepsis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms associated with different antibiotic regimens for early-onset neonatal sepsis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase Ovid, CINAHL, LILACS, Science Citation Index EXPANDED, and Conference Proceedings Citation Index – Science, with the last search performed on March 12, 2021. Additional searches were conducted in clinical trial registries and reference lists of retrieved articles to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs. The inclusion criteria for this review were RCTs that compared different antibiotic regimens for early-onset neonatal sepsis. Participants were neonates randomized within the first 72 hours of life. Data collection and analysis were performed independently by three review authors, who assessed study eligibility, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The GRADE approach was used to determine the certainty of the evidence. The primary outcome of interest was all-cause mortality, while secondary outcomes included serious adverse events, respiratory support, circulatory support, nephrotoxicity, neurological developmental impairment, necrotizing enterocolitis, and ototoxicity. The primary time point for outcome assessment was at the maximum follow-up period. The review included five RCTs involving a total of 865 participants. All included trials were determined to have a high risk of bias, and the certainty of the evidence, as assessed using the GRADE approach, was very low. The trials evaluated five different antibiotic regimen comparisons: (1) ampicillin plus gentamicin versus benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, (2) piperacillin plus tazobactam versus amikacin, (3) ticarcillin plus clavulanic acid versus piperacillin plus gentamicin, (4) piperacillin versus ampicillin plus amikacin, and (5) ceftazidime versus benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin. None of the five comparisons demonstrated evidence of a difference in outcomes such as all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, circulatory support, nephrotoxicity, neurological developmental impairment, or necrotizing enterocolitis. However, none of the trials were adequately powered to provide robust evidence regarding the comparative benefits and risks of any specific antibiotic regimen. Additionally, none of the trials assessed respiratory support or ototoxicity. Due to the lack of sufficient data, no meta-analyses were conducted. The findings of this review highlight the uncertainty surrounding the benefits and harms of different antibiotic regimens for early-onset neonatal sepsis. The evidence is insufficient to conclude that any particular antibiotic regimen is superior to another. The authors emphasize the need for large, well-designed RCTs with a low risk of bias to better assess the comparative effectiveness and safety of various antibiotic regimens in this population.
